title: Linux Administration Quiz
description: Test your Linux command-line, system administration, and troubleshooting skills.

questions.question: Which command shows disk usage of each directory summarized?
questions.explain: 'du -sh /*' summarizes disk usage per top-level directory in human-readable form, unlike df which reports filesystem-level usage.

questions.question: What does 'chmod 755 script.sh' set?
options: A. Owner: rwx, Group: r-x, Others: r-x
B. Owner: rwx, Group: rwx, Others: rwx
C. Owner: rw-, Group: r--, Others: r--
D. Owner: rwx, Group: r--, Others: ---
questions.explain: 755 in octal is 7=rwx for owner, 5=r-x for group, 5=r-x for others, since each digit sums read(4)+write(2)+execute(1).

questions.question: In LVM, what is the correct order of creation?
questions.explain: Physical volumes (PV) are pooled into a volume group (VG), from which logical volumes (LV) are then carved out.

questions.question: Which command shows TCP listening ports with process names?
questions.explain: 'ss -tlnp' lists TCP (t) listening (l) sockets numerically (n) with the owning process (p), replacing the older netstat.

questions.question: What does 'set -euo pipefail' do in a bash script?
options: A. Sets environment variables for production
B. Exit on error, treat unset vars as errors, fail on pipe errors
C. Sets file permissions for the script
questions.explain: -e exits on any command failure, -u errors on unset variables, and pipefail makes a pipeline fail if any stage fails, improving script safety.

questions.question: Which systemd command shows the last 50 lines of nginx service logs?
questions.explain: journalctl -u filters logs by systemd unit, and -n 50 limits output to the most recent 50 journal entries for that service.

questions.question: What does SUID bit do on an executable file?
options: A. Allows any user to delete the file
B. The file runs with the file owner's permissions, not the executing user's
C. Prevents the file from being executed by others
D. Sets the file as a system-critical binary
questions.explain: The Set User ID bit makes the process run with the privileges of the file's owner (e.g. root) rather than the invoking user.

questions.question: What command displays SELinux security contexts on files?
questions.explain: 'ls -Z' adds the SELinux security context (user:role:type:level) to normal file listing output.

questions.question: How do you extend an ext4 logical volume online without unmounting?
questions.explain: lvextend grows the logical volume's size, then resize2fs grows the ext4 filesystem to fill it, both supported while mounted.

questions.question: What is RAID 5 minimum disk requirement and how many disk failures can it survive?
questions.explain: RAID 5 stripes data with distributed parity across a minimum of 3 disks, allowing the array to survive exactly one disk failure.

questions.question: Which SSH option creates a local port forward (access remote service locally)?
questions.explain: -L forwards a local port to a port on the remote side, letting you reach a remote-only service through your local machine.

questions.question: What does the sticky bit on /tmp prevent?
options: A. Creating new files in the directory
B. Only allows the file owner or root to delete/rename their own files, even if others have write permission
C. Makes the directory read-only for everyone
D. Prevents all executables in the directory from running
questions.explain: The sticky bit restricts deletion/renaming in a shared, world-writable directory to the file's owner or root, protecting other users' files.

questions.question: What does 'getenforce' return when SELinux is actively blocking violations?
questions.explain: 'Enforcing' means SELinux actively denies and logs policy violations, as opposed to 'Permissive' which only logs them.

questions.question: Which command shows the process tree with PIDs?
questions.explain: pstree displays processes as a hierarchical parent-child tree, and the -p flag adds each process's PID.

questions.question: What does 'kill -HUP PID' signal do to a running process?
options: A. Force kills the process immediately (SIGKILL)
C. Sends SIGHUP — typically causes the process to reload its configuration
questions.explain: Many daemons intercept SIGHUP (signal 1) to re-read their config files without a full restart, a convention inherited from terminal hangups.

questions.question: In /etc/passwd, what does 'x' in the password field mean?
options: C. The hashed password is stored in /etc/shadow
questions.explain: 'x' is a placeholder indicating the real hashed password lives in /etc/shadow, which unlike /etc/passwd is not world-readable.

questions.question: What is the USE method for Linux performance analysis?
options: B. Utilization, Saturation, Errors — check each for every resource
C. User, System, Exit codes per process
questions.explain: The USE method (Brendan Gregg) systematically checks Utilization, Saturation, and Errors for every system resource to find bottlenecks.

questions.question: Which file defines filesystem mounts that persist across reboots?
questions.explain: /etc/fstab lists filesystems, their mount points, and mount options that the system reads at boot to mount them automatically.

questions.question: What does 'chattr +i /etc/resolv.conf' do to the file?
options: A. Makes the file executable by all users
B. Makes the file immutable — even root cannot modify or delete it
C. Sets the file as hidden from ls output
D. Changes file to inherit parent directory's permissions
questions.explain: The immutable attribute blocks all modification, deletion, or renaming of the file at the filesystem level, overriding normal permissions.

questions.question: What does 'nginx -t' do?
options: A. Tests connectivity to upstream servers
B. Starts nginx in test mode with minimal traffic
C. Validates nginx configuration file syntax without starting
D. Shows nginx active connections and throughput
questions.explain: '-t' parses and checks the configuration files for syntax errors and reports the result without actually starting the server.

questions.question: Which cron expression runs a job every day at 3:30 AM?
questions.explain: Cron fields are minute hour day month weekday, so '30 3 * * *' means minute 30 of hour 3, i.e. 3:30 AM every day.

questions.question: With default umask 022, what permissions do newly created files get?
questions.explain: Files start from a base of 666 (no execute); subtracting umask 022 removes write for group and others, yielding 644.

questions.question: How do you permanently allow port 8080 for Nginx in SELinux?
questions.explain: semanage port adds a TCP port to the http_port_t type's allowed list persistently, which SELinux policy requires httpd to bind to it.

questions.question: What does 'lvextend -l +100%FREE /dev/vg/lv' do?
options: A. Extends the logical volume by 100MB
B. Extends the LV to use all free space remaining in the volume group
C. Extends the volume group by 100% of current size
D. Creates a new logical volume using 100% of the disk
questions.explain: The -l flag with %FREE sizes the LV relative to available extents, so +100%FREE consumes all remaining free space in the VG.

questions.question: Which systemd unit type replaces traditional cron jobs?
options: D. .timer unit paired with a .service unit
questions.explain: A .timer unit schedules activation and triggers a matching .service unit, giving systemd-native dependency and logging integration unlike cron.
